title: The boy far from home
hookLine: Duleep Singh, still a child, is raised by British guardians and baptized a Christian

lines: A BOY WHO WAS A MAHARAJA.
cards: A garden by the Ganges at Fatehgarh, a long way from Lahore. A boy with a pony, a tutor, a few servants, and a Scottish doctor who has been put in charge of him. The boy has been a Maharaja.
He has sat on his father's throne, been bowed to by generals, worn the jewels of the Punjab. Now he has lessons, a garden and guardians. His mother has been sent away, and the court he knew is gone.

teach.b: After the annexation, Duleep Singh was placed in the care of Dr. John Login, who had looked after the treasury at Lahore. Login and his wife, Lena, raised him.
Her later book about the boy is warm toward him, and also plainly written from the guardians' side.
He was taken out of the Punjab to Fatehgarh, away from the Sikh court, the gurdwaras of Lahore, and anyone who might raise him as a Sikh king.
The British saw a boy who could become a rallying point, so they kept him far away.

In those years, a boy in his early teens, Duleep Singh asked to become a Christian, and he was baptized. The Login account says the wish was his own, that he'd been listening to a household servant read from the Bible.
Some Sikh writers see it differently: a child cut off from his mother, his faith and his people, shaped by the only adults left around him.
Both readings are still held, and the sources can't fully settle what was in a child's heart.

teach.h: THE HOT WIND DOES NOT TOUCH.
teach.b: In a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Bilaval, the Guru says the hot wind does not touch the one who shelters in the Lord: a protecting line is drawn on every side, and no pain comes near.
Those words were there all along, in the scripture of the faith he was raised away from.

how: Sikh histories tell Duleep Singh's childhood under British guardianship as part of the loss of the kingdom, and his baptism is read differently in different accounts: as his own choice, or as the result of being separated from his mother and his faith.

games.q: you're a British official after the annexation. the boy Maharaja could become a rallying point. what do you do, as the histories tell it?

practice: Go back to a night when you were young and away from home, a sleepover, a hospital bed, a camp, a new house, and remember what helped, if anything did: a voice, a light left on, something from home in your hands.
Hold that small thing in mind, then let a child who is far from home today come to mind, and wish them the same. If you pray, hold that child before Waheguru as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sarnai, sanctuary or shelter, where the hot wind cannot touch the one within: Duleep Singh, a Maharaja no longer, raised by British guardians at Fatehgarh. Today's word.
